newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major subpoenaed in libel case.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major subpoenaed in libel case.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major received a summons on Thursday to give evidence in court in a libel case involving one of his members of parliament.

The case is expected to go to court in October and could mean that Major and Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine, who was also subpoenaed, could miss part of their Conservative Party's annual conference.
If he attends, Major will be the first British Prime Minister to have given evidence in a court case.
Former trade minister Neil Hamilton is suing the Guardian newspaper over its claims that he accepted money in exchange for asking questions in parliament.
Major said he had been taken by surprise by the subpoena, issued by lawyers for the Guardian.
"The first I heard of it was first thing this morning. I'm often surprised when I open the newspapers. Today was one of those days," Major told reporters.
Thursday's Sun newspaper said Major would be called to give evidence in court, but the Guardian confirmed the subpoenas only late on Thursday.

Hamilton resigned as trade minister in 1994 over the allegations that he accepted cash in return for asking parliamentary questions on behalf of Mohammed al-Fayed, the owner of London's prestigious Harrods department store.
He protested that he was the victim of a "foully motivated rumour and a media witchhunt" and is reported to be seeking one million pounds ($1.5 million) in damages from the Guardian.
Two senior civil servants have also been summoned to give evidence.
